title: Domain 1: System Management
description: Original practice items written against the published XK0-006 objectives for domain 1. These are not exam questions and no part of them is drawn from any real exam.

questions.prompt: A script must run identically whether it is started by cron, by systemd, or from an interactive shell. Which statement about the shell environment is correct?

options.text: Cron runs the script with a reduced environment, so PATH may differ from an interactive login
Cron sources /etc/profile before running a job, so the environment matches a login shell
Exported variables are inherited by every process on the system once they are set
A script always inherits the environment of the user who owns the file

questions.explanation: Cron gives a job a deliberately minimal environment. PATH is short, most variables set in a login shell are absent, and a command that works when typed can fail under cron for no other reason. The fix is to set what the script needs explicitly or to use absolute paths. Sourcing /etc/profile is what a login shell does, not what cron does, which is exactly why the two environments differ. Exporting a variable makes it available to that shell's children only, not to unrelated processes. And a script inherits the environment of the process that started it, not of the file's owner, which is why the same file behaves differently depending on who or what launched it.

questions.prompt: A server has a 4 TB disk that will hold a single filesystem, and the partition table must support it. Which partitioning scheme is required?

options.text: GPT, because MBR cannot address beyond 2 TB with 512-byte sectors
MBR, because it supports up to four primary partitions of any size
Either, because the partition table does not limit filesystem size
MBR with an extended partition, which removes the size limit

questions.explanation: MBR stores block addresses in 32 bits, so with 512-byte sectors it cannot describe anything past roughly 2 TB. GPT uses 64-bit addressing and has no practical limit at this scale. The four-primary-partition limit in MBR is real but it is a count, not a size, so it does not help here. The partition table does constrain what can be addressed, so saying it is irrelevant to size is the misconception being tested. Extended partitions raise the number of partitions available and do nothing about the addressing limit.

questions.prompt: A logical volume needs another 50 GB and its volume group has free extents. Which sequence completes the change so the extra space is usable?

options.text: Extend the logical volume, then grow the filesystem on it
Grow the filesystem, then extend the logical volume beneath it
Extend the volume group, which resizes its logical volumes automatically
Unmount the volume, recreate it at the larger size, and restore from backup

questions.explanation: The block device has to get bigger before the filesystem can be told to use the extra space, so lvextend comes first and resize2fs or xfs_growfs second. Reversing them fails because the filesystem cannot grow past the end of the device it sits on. Extending a volume group adds capacity to the pool and never resizes a logical volume by itself, which is the step people expect to be automatic and is not. Recreating and restoring works and is a great deal of downtime for an operation that is online and takes seconds, which is much of the reason LVM exists.

questions.prompt: An administrator adds an optional data volume to /etc/fstab. The machine must still finish booting when that disk is missing. Which mount option achieves that?

options.text: nofail
noauto
defaults
ro

questions.explanation: nofail tells systemd to attempt the mount and to carry on booting if it fails, which is exactly the requirement. noauto is close enough to be tempting and does something different: it stops the mount being attempted at boot at all, so the volume is never mounted even when the disk is present. defaults includes auto, so a missing disk blocks local-fs.target and drops the machine to emergency mode. ro controls whether the filesystem is writable and has no bearing on whether a failure is tolerated.

questions.prompt: Which RAID level provides redundancy through a single parity block distributed across all members, allowing one drive to fail?

options.text: RAID 5
RAID 0
RAID 1
RAID 6

questions.explanation: RAID 5 stripes data with one parity block per stripe, spread across the members, and survives losing one drive. RAID 0 stripes with no parity at all, so it improves throughput and reduces reliability. RAID 1 gives redundancy by mirroring rather than by parity, so no parity block is involved. RAID 6 is the deliberate near-miss: it uses two parity blocks and tolerates two failures, which is the same idea with different arithmetic.

questions.prompt: A host has an address of 10.4.7.20/22. Which statement about that configuration is correct?

options.text: The host treats 10.4.4.0 through 10.4.7.255 as directly reachable
The host treats only 10.4.7.0 through 10.4.7.255 as directly reachable
The prefix length affects routing but not which addresses are considered local
A /22 is invalid because prefix lengths must be multiples of 8

questions.explanation: A /22 covers four /24 blocks, so the network runs from 10.4.4.0 to 10.4.7.255 and the host will resolve any address in that range on the local link rather than sending it to a gateway. Reading it as a single /24 is the common error, and it produces a machine that cannot reach neighbours it should be able to reach directly. The prefix is precisely what decides local against remote, so treating it as routing-only inverts the mechanism. Prefix lengths are not restricted to multiples of 8, which is the whole point of classless addressing.

questions.prompt: Which command shows whether a network interface has carrier, meaning something is connected at the other end?

options.text: ip link show, and look for LOWER_UP in the flags
ip addr show, and look for an assigned address
ip route show, and look for a default route
ping the gateway and see whether it answers

questions.explanation: LOWER_UP in the flags means the driver sees carrier, so an interface that is UP without it is enabled and unplugged. An address can be configured on an interface with no cable attached, so its presence proves nothing about the physical link. A default route is a routing table entry and exists regardless of whether any interface is connected. Pinging the gateway is a reasonable test of a working path and cannot distinguish a missing cable from a firewall, a wrong address, or an unresponsive gateway.

questions.prompt: An archive must preserve ownership, permissions, and symbolic links, and be restorable on another Linux host. Which approach is appropriate?

options.text: tar, which records ownership, modes, and links in the archive
gzip on each file, which compresses without changing metadata
zip, which is the portable choice for Unix permissions
cp -r into a directory, then compress the directory

questions.explanation: tar was designed for exactly this: it stores ownership, mode bits, timestamps, and link structure alongside the data, and it is the reason it remains the default for Linux backups. gzip compresses a single stream and has no concept of ownership or of more than one file, so it is a complement to tar rather than an alternative. zip is portable in the sense of running everywhere and its handling of Unix ownership is inconsistent, which is what makes it the plausible wrong answer. cp -r without -a drops ownership and can follow symlinks rather than preserving them, so metadata is already lost before anything is compressed.

questions.prompt: A full backup runs on Sunday. Each weekday backup must capture only what changed since the previous day's backup, keeping each day's job as small as possible. Which strategy is described?

options.text: Incremental, where each backup captures changes since the last backup of any kind
Differential, where each backup captures changes since the last full backup
Full, taken daily with compression to keep the size down
Snapshot, which records only the blocks that differ from the live volume

questions.explanation: Incremental is defined by its reference point: each run captures what changed since the previous backup whatever type it was, which keeps every weekday job small and makes a restore require the full plus every incremental in order. Differential is the near-miss and always references the last full backup, so its jobs grow through the week while a restore needs only two pieces. A daily full ignores the requirement to capture only changes. A snapshot is a point-in-time view of a volume rather than a backup strategy, and on its own it does not protect against losing the volume.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes a container from a virtual machine?

options.text: A container shares the host kernel; a virtual machine runs its own
A container runs its own kernel; a virtual machine shares the host kernel
A container cannot have its own network namespace or filesystem
A virtual machine is always faster to start because it is smaller

questions.explanation: The kernel is the dividing line. Containers are processes on the host kernel isolated by namespaces and cgroups, while a virtual machine is given virtual hardware and boots a kernel of its own, which is what lets it run a different operating system. Reversing the two is the misconception worth testing directly. Containers do get their own network namespace and filesystem view, and those are what make them feel like separate machines. Virtual machines are generally slower to start and larger, because a full boot is involved, so the last option inverts the usual trade.

questions.prompt: Which directory does the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard designate for variable data that a program writes during normal operation, such as logs and spool files?

options.text: /var
/etc
/usr
/opt

questions.explanation: /var holds data that changes while the system runs, which is why logs, spool directories, and caches live there and why it is often given its own filesystem so a runaway log cannot fill the root. /etc is configuration, which is local and expected to be relatively static. /usr is shareable read-only program data, and the modern convention is that it can be mounted read-only entirely. /opt is for add-on application packages that keep their files together rather than distributing them across the hierarchy.

questions.prompt: After attaching a new disk to a running server, which command lists block devices so the administrator can confirm the kernel detected it?

options.text: lsblk
lsmod
lsof
df

questions.explanation: lsblk lists block devices and their partitions in a tree, which answers whether the kernel has seen the disk at all and is the right first check. lsmod lists loaded kernel modules, which is relevant if the driver is missing and does not itself show devices. lsof lists open files and has nothing to say about hardware that has just appeared. df reports filesystem usage, so it only shows devices that already carry a mounted filesystem, which a brand new disk does not.

questions.prompt: A command typed at the prompt behaves differently from the same name run inside a script. Which resolution order does the shell use when deciding what to run?

options.text: Alias, then function, then builtin, then a match in PATH
PATH first, then builtin, then function, then alias
Builtin first, then PATH, and aliases are never consulted
Whichever match appears first alphabetically in PATH

questions.explanation: The shell resolves a name as alias, then function, then builtin, then a search of PATH, and that order is why a command can behave one way interactively and another way in a script where aliases are not loaded. Putting PATH first inverts the mechanism and would make it impossible to override a program with a function. Aliases are consulted, and in fact they win, which is the whole reason an alias can shadow a real program. PATH is searched in the order its directories are listed rather than alphabetically, so an earlier directory wins regardless of name.

questions.prompt: A newly installed network card is listed by lspci but no interface appears. Which check is the appropriate next step?

options.text: lspci -k, to see whether a kernel driver has bound to the device
ip addr, to assign the interface an address
systemctl restart network, to force the stack to re-enumerate
ethtool, to negotiate the link speed

questions.explanation: Enumeration on the bus and a driver claiming the device are two different steps, and lspci -k shows which drivers are bound. A device with no driver line is the classic present-but-not-working case, usually a missing module or missing firmware. Assigning an address needs an interface to exist first, so ip addr has nothing to act on. Restarting the network service manages interfaces that already exist and does not create one for an unclaimed device. ethtool queries an interface, so it also depends on the step that has not happened yet.

questions.prompt: Which statement about creating a filesystem on a new partition is correct?

options.text: mkfs writes filesystem metadata and destroys any data already on the partition
mkfs adjusts the partition table so the partition can hold a filesystem
mkfs must be run on the whole disk rather than on a partition
mkfs preserves existing data and only adds the superblock

questions.explanation: mkfs lays down a new filesystem structure over whatever was there, so it is destructive and there is no undo. It does not touch the partition table, which is fdisk, parted, or gdisk territory, and confusing the two is the reason people expect mkfs to resize something. A filesystem can be created on a whole disk without partitioning it, which is common for LVM physical volumes and for some virtual disks, so requiring the whole disk is wrong in the other direction. Nothing about mkfs preserves existing data.

questions.prompt: An application cannot resolve an internal hostname, and dig against a public resolver returns nothing for it. Which check reflects what the application will actually experience?

options.text: getent hosts, which uses the same resolution path the application does
dig against the same public resolver, repeated to rule out a transient failure
ping the hostname, since a reply proves resolution succeeded
nslookup with the type set to ANY

questions.explanation: getent goes through the C library, so it reads /etc/hosts and honours the source order in nsswitch.conf exactly as the application does. dig speaks DNS directly and skips both, which is why it can disagree with the application and why repeating it adds nothing. ping does resolve the name through the library and mixes resolution with reachability, so a failure does not tell you which half broke. Asking for ANY records is largely ignored by modern resolvers and still bypasses the library path that matters here.

questions.prompt: A command must have both its normal output and its error messages written to the same file. Which redirection does that?

options.text: command > out.log 2>&1
command 2>&1 > out.log
command > out.log > 2.log
command | tee out.log

questions.explanation: Redirections are processed left to right, so sending stdout to the file first and then pointing stderr at wherever stdout now goes captures both. Reversing the order is the classic mistake: stderr is aimed at the terminal, which is where stdout still points at that moment, and only then does stdout move to the file, so errors continue to the screen. Two output redirections do not merge streams; the second simply supersedes the first for stdout. tee copies stdout to a file and to the screen and leaves stderr untouched.

questions.prompt: A log file has colon-separated fields and the third field must be extracted from every line. Which approach is appropriate?

options.text: awk -F: '{print $3}'
grep -o ':.*:' to isolate the middle of the line
sed 's/:/ /g' to convert the file to a single field
sort -t: -k3 to bring the third field to the front

questions.explanation: awk splits each line on a delimiter and addresses fields by number, which is precisely the job. grep matches text and has no concept of fields, so a pattern like that returns whatever happens to sit between the first and last colon rather than one field. Replacing the delimiters with sed destroys the structure you need to select by position. sort with a field key orders lines by that field and never extracts it, so the output is the same lines in a different sequence.

questions.prompt: A backup policy states an RPO of one hour and an RTO of four hours. Which pair of statements describes what those commit to?

options.text: At most one hour of data may be lost, and service must be restored within four hours
At most four hours of data may be lost, and service must be restored within one hour
Backups run hourly and are verified every four hours
Backups are retained for one hour and archived after four

questions.explanation: RPO is about data and looks backwards from the incident: it caps how much work may be lost, which sets how often backups must run. RTO is about time and looks forwards: it caps how long the service may be down, which drives the restore mechanism rather than the backup schedule. Swapping them is the error the question exists to catch. Backup frequency follows from RPO but the objective is not a schedule, and neither term says anything about verification cadence or retention, which are separate policies.

questions.prompt: Which description matches a type 1 hypervisor?

options.text: It runs directly on the hardware, with no general-purpose operating system beneath it
It runs as an application on top of a general-purpose operating system
It shares the host kernel with the guests it runs
It runs only paravirtualised guests that have been modified for it

questions.explanation: A type 1 hypervisor sits on the bare metal and schedules guests itself, which is why it is used where density and isolation matter. A type 2 hypervisor runs as a program on an existing operating system, which is convenient on a workstation and adds a layer. Sharing the host kernel describes containers rather than any hypervisor, and mixing the two models is the common confusion. Paravirtualisation is a technique some hypervisors support and is not what defines the type.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the root account is correct on a standard Linux system?

options.text: Root is identified by UID 0, so any account with UID 0 has the same privilege
Root is identified by the name root, so renaming the account removes its privilege
Root privilege comes from membership of the wheel group
Root is subject to file permission bits in the same way as other users

questions.explanation: The kernel checks the numeric UID, so privilege follows UID 0 and a second account created with that UID is equally powerful, which is why auditing for extra UID 0 entries is worth doing. The name is a label in /etc/passwd and carries no authority, so renaming changes nothing. The wheel group commonly grants the ability to use sudo, which is a route to privilege rather than the source of it. Root bypasses the ordinary read, write, and execute checks through its capabilities, which is exactly why testing a permissions problem as root tells you nothing.

questions.prompt: Which command shows the absolute path of the shell's current working directory?

options.text: pwd
cd
ls -d
dirname

questions.explanation: pwd prints the working directory, which is the process attribute the shell tracks. cd changes it and prints nothing on success. ls -d lists a directory entry itself rather than its contents, so it shows a name rather than a full path. dirname strips the last component from a string it is given and never inspects where the shell currently is.

questions.prompt: Which command shows the last part of a file and keeps printing as the file grows?

options.text: tail -f
head -f
cat -f
less -f

questions.explanation: tail -f prints the end and follows additions, which is why it is the reflex for watching a log. head reads from the start and has no follow mode, so the option pairs a real command with a flag it lacks. cat prints once and exits, with no ability to wait for more. less -f forces opening a special file and does not follow; the follow key inside less is a separate feature.

questions.prompt: Which manual section documents configuration file formats?

options.text: Section 5
Section 1
Section 8
Section 3

questions.explanation: Section 5 covers file formats, which is why man 5 sshd_config explains the file while man sshd covers the daemon. Section 1 is user commands, the default when no number is given. Section 8 is administration commands, so it holds the daemon rather than its configuration. Section 3 is library calls, aimed at programmers rather than administrators.

questions.prompt: Which command lists currently loaded kernel modules?

options.text: lsmod
lspci
lsblk
lsusb

questions.explanation: lsmod reads the list of modules the kernel has loaded, along with their use counts. lspci enumerates devices on the PCI bus and says nothing about which drivers are loaded unless -k is added. lsblk lists block devices, which is storage rather than modules. lsusb does the same for USB devices.

questions.prompt: Which command loads a kernel module and its dependencies by name?

options.text: modprobe
insmod
depmod
modinfo

questions.explanation: modprobe resolves dependencies from the module map and loads what is needed, which is why it is the command to use. insmod loads a single file and fails if the module needs another, so it is the lower-level tool. depmod rebuilds the dependency map rather than loading anything. modinfo reports a module's parameters and description without loading it.

questions.prompt: Which command validates /etc/fstab entries without rebooting?

options.text: findmnt --verify
fsck -n
mount --fake
systemctl status local-fs.target

questions.explanation: findmnt --verify parses the file and reports problems, which is the check to run before a reboot rather than after. fsck examines a filesystem's structure and has nothing to say about the fstab entry that names it. mount --fake goes through the motions without mounting and does not validate the whole file. Checking the target reports what happened at the last boot rather than what the current file would do.

questions.prompt: In LVM, what is a physical extent?

options.text: The fixed-size allocation unit a group is split into
A whole disk after it is added to a volume group
A partition that has been formatted with a filesystem
The largest size a logical volume is allowed to reach

questions.explanation: A volume group is carved into physical extents of a fixed size, and logical volumes are built from them, which is why volume sizes are always a multiple of that unit. A whole disk added to the group is a physical volume rather than an extent. A formatted partition is a filesystem on a device and sits above LVM entirely. No fixed ceiling applies to a logical volume beyond the free extents available.

questions.prompt: Which statement about RAID and backups is correct?

options.text: RAID protects against drive failure, not against deletion or corruption
RAID removes the need for backups once parity is in use
RAID protects against accidental deletion because parity can rebuild it
RAID and backup provide the same protection at different speeds

questions.explanation: RAID keeps a service running through a hardware failure, and it replicates every write faithfully, including the one that deleted the wrong directory. Backups exist for the mistakes and the corruption RAID copies. Treating parity as a backup is the belief that loses data, because parity rebuilds a failed member rather than a previous state. The two address different risks rather than the same one at different speeds.

questions.prompt: Which command shows the routing table on a modern Linux system?

options.text: ip route
ifconfig -a
netstat -i
ip addr

questions.explanation: ip route lists the routes the kernel will use, including the default. ifconfig shows interface configuration, is deprecated, and never displayed routes. netstat -i shows interface statistics rather than routing, and netstat itself is superseded by ss. ip addr shows addresses on interfaces, which is the neighbouring subcommand and a different question.

questions.prompt: Which port does SSH listen on by default?
questions.explanation: SSH uses TCP 22. Port 23 is telnet, the unencrypted predecessor SSH replaced, which is why the two are adjacent and easy to confuse. Port 25 is SMTP for mail transfer. Port 21 is the FTP control channel, another cleartext protocol from the same era.

questions.prompt: What does export do to a shell variable?

options.text: Marks it to be passed into the environment of child processes
Writes it to a file so it persists across logins
Makes it readable by every user on the system
Converts it to a read-only constant

questions.explanation: export marks a variable for inclusion in the environment handed to processes the shell starts, which is why a script cannot see a variable that was only set. Persistence across logins comes from a startup file such as .bashrc rather than from export. Other users cannot read another shell's variables, so visibility does not widen. Making a variable read-only is what readonly does.

questions.prompt: What does the pipe operator connect?

options.text: The standard output of one command to the standard input of the next
The standard error of one command to the input of the next
Both output streams of one command into a file
Two commands so they run in parallel without sharing data

questions.explanation: A pipe wires stdout into the next command's stdin, which is why errors still appear on the terminal and why 2>&1 is needed to include them. Connecting stderr instead is what people expect when they wonder why error text is not being filtered by a grep. Sending both streams to a file is redirection rather than a pipe. The commands do run concurrently, and the point of the construct is that they share a data stream.

questions.prompt: Which command replaces every occurrence of a string in a stream?

options.text: sed 's/old/new/g'
sed 's/old/new/'
grep -r 'old' 'new'
tr 'old' 'new'

questions.explanation: The g flag makes the substitution apply to every match on a line rather than only the first, which is the difference between the first two options and a very common oversight. grep selects lines and cannot modify them, so the second argument is read as a file name. tr translates single characters rather than strings, so it maps o to n and so on rather than replacing a word.

questions.prompt: Which command extracts a gzip-compressed tar archive?

options.text: tar -xzf archive.tar.gz
tar -czf archive.tar.gz
gzip -d archive.tar.gz | tar
tar -tzf archive.tar.gz

questions.explanation: x extracts, z handles the gzip layer, and f names the file. Using c instead creates an archive, which overwrites the file you meant to read, and that single letter is the difference between reading and destroying. Decompressing separately then piping into tar without an option leaves tar no instruction about what to do. The t flag lists contents without extracting, which is a useful check and not extraction.

questions.prompt: Why is a restore test an essential part of a backup policy?

options.text: A backup that has never been restored is an untested assumption
Restoring compacts the archive and reclaims space
Restoring is required to advance the incremental chain
Restoring refreshes the retention period on the stored copy

questions.explanation: Backups fail quietly: a job reports success while writing an empty archive, excluding the database, or producing something the restore tool cannot read. Only a restore proves otherwise, and the time to discover a problem is not during an incident. Restoring does not compact anything, since it reads rather than writes the archive. Incremental chains advance from backups rather than restores. Retention is a policy applied to stored copies and is unaffected by reading one.

questions.prompt: What does a hypervisor provide to a guest operating system?

options.text: Virtual hardware, including CPU, memory, and devices
A shared kernel that the guest processes run on
A filesystem namespace isolated from the host
A container runtime for packaging applications

questions.explanation: A hypervisor presents virtual hardware, so the guest boots its own kernel and can be a different operating system entirely. Sharing a kernel describes containers, which is the distinction worth holding firmly. An isolated filesystem namespace is also a container mechanism and is only part of what a guest gets. A container runtime is a different layer that may run on top of a virtual machine but is not what a hypervisor offers.

questions.prompt: Which storage arrangement lets several virtual machines start from one base image while keeping their changes separate?

options.text: Thin-provisioned images layered over a common backing file
A single shared image mounted read-write by every guest
One full copy of the image per guest, created at boot
A read-only image with all writes discarded at shutdown

questions.explanation: A backing file holds the shared base and each guest writes into its own overlay, so disk use stays low and the guests do not interfere. Sharing one writable image lets guests corrupt each other's filesystems, since none of them expects another writer. Full copies work and cost the full size for every guest, which is what layering avoids. Discarding writes describes a stateless or kiosk arrangement rather than a way to keep changes separate.

questions.prompt: A device appears under /dev after being attached. Which subsystem created that node?

options.text: udev, acting on kernel uevents
systemd-journald, from the kernel log
The filesystem driver for the device
The bootloader, which enumerates hardware

questions.explanation: The kernel emits a uevent when a device appears and udev applies rules to create the node with the right name, ownership, and any symlinks. journald records log entries and creates nothing under /dev. A filesystem driver mounts a filesystem on a device that already exists as a node. The bootloader runs long before this and has no role once the system is up.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a filesystem UUID is correct?

options.text: It belongs to the filesystem and survives the device being renamed
It belongs to the partition and changes when the filesystem is created
It is assigned by the kernel at each boot from the discovery order
It is the same for every filesystem created by the same tool

questions.explanation: The UUID is written into the filesystem's metadata when it is created, so it follows the data regardless of whether the kernel calls the device sdb or sdc today. That stability is exactly why fstab should use it. The identifier is a property of the filesystem rather than the partition, and creating a new filesystem generates a new one. Nothing is assigned per boot, which is the behaviour of device names and the problem UUIDs solve. Each filesystem gets a distinct value.

questions.prompt: What does a DNS record's TTL control?

options.text: How long a resolver may cache the answer before asking again
How long the authoritative server keeps the record
How many hops a query may traverse before failing
How long a client waits before treating a query as failed

questions.explanation: TTL is a caching instruction, so it decides how long an answer may be reused and therefore how long a change takes to become visible everywhere. It says nothing about retention on the authoritative server, which holds the record until it is edited. Hop limits belong to IP rather than DNS. A client's patience is a resolver timeout, configured locally and unrelated to the record.

questions.prompt: Which practice protects backups against ransomware that reaches the backup server?

options.text: Keeping one copy offline or immutable, so it cannot be altered
Encrypting the backups, so the attacker cannot read them
Increasing backup frequency, so less data is lost
Storing backups on a separate filesystem on the same host

questions.explanation: An attacker with access to writable backups deletes or encrypts them, so the copy that saves you is the one nothing online can change: offline media, or storage with immutability enforced. Encryption protects confidentiality and does nothing to stop deletion. More frequent backups reduce data loss from an ordinary failure and give an attacker more copies to destroy. A separate filesystem on the same host shares its fate.
